questions.text:
Consider the function [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] defined as follows:

[latex] f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lr} c_{1} e^{x}-c_{2} \log _{{e}}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), & \text { if } x>0 \\ 3 & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right. [/latex]

where [latex]c_{1}, c_{2} \in \mathbb{R}[/latex].

If [latex]f[/latex] is continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], then [latex]c_{1}+c_{2}=[/latex] ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
For [latex]f[/latex] to be continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], we need [latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)=f(0)=3[/latex].

[latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\left[c_1e^{x}-c_2\log_e\left(\dfrac1x\right)\right][/latex]

As [latex]x\to0^{+}[/latex]: [latex]e^{x}\to1[/latex], while [latex]\log_e(1/x)=-\log_e x\to+\infty[/latex]. For the overall limit to be a finite number, the coefficient of this diverging term must be zero:
[latex]c_2=0[/latex].

With [latex]c_2=0[/latex], the limit becomes [latex]c_1\cdot1=c_1[/latex]. Setting this equal to [latex]f(0)=3[/latex] gives [latex]c_1=3[/latex].

So [latex]c_1+c_2=3+0=3[/latex].

Answer: 3

questions.text:
Let [latex]n>1[/latex]. Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix [latex]M[/latex] with its elements from [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex]. Let the vector [latex](0,1,0,0, \ldots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}[/latex] be in the null space of [latex]M[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are always correct?
questions.solution:
Since [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex] is in the null space of [latex]M[/latex], we have [latex]M\cdot(0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T=\mathbf{0}[/latex]. But [latex]M[/latex] times this unit vector simply extracts the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex]. So the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex] is entirely zero.

- Determinant: A matrix with an all-zero column always has determinant [latex]0[/latex]. So "[latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]" is always true. ("[latex]\det(M)=1[/latex]" is always false.)
- Rank: The rank could be anywhere from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]n-1[/latex] depending on the other columns, so "rank [latex]=1[/latex]" is not always true.
- Null space size: Since the null space contains the nonzero vector [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], it also contains every scalar multiple of it (e.g. [latex](0,2,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], [latex](0,-1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], etc.), giving infinitely many, hence at least two, distinct non-zero vectors in the null space. This is always true.

Answer: Determinant of M is 0; and there are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of M.

questions.text: For [latex]n>1[/latex], the maximum multiplicity of any eigenvalue of an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix with elements from [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex] is
questions.solution:
For an [latex]n\times n[/latex] real matrix, the multiplicity of any eigenvalue (as a root of the characteristic polynomial, which has degree [latex]n[/latex]) can be at most [latex]n[/latex].

This bound is achieved: for example, the identity matrix [latex]I_n[/latex] (or any scalar matrix [latex]cI_n[/latex]) has the single eigenvalue [latex]c[/latex] repeated exactly [latex]n[/latex] times.

So the maximum possible multiplicity of any eigenvalue is [latex]n[/latex].

Answer: n

questions.text: Consider [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrices with their elements from [latex]\{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\}[/latex]. The number of such matrices with even number of [latex]\mathbf{1}[/latex] s in every row and every column is
questions.solution:
We need [latex]4\times4[/latex] binary matrices where every row and every column has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s.

Freely choose the top-left [latex]3\times3[/latex] sub-block: this can be filled in any of [latex]2^{9}=512[/latex] ways.

Once this [latex]3\times3[/latex] block is fixed, the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th column (for the first [latex]3[/latex] rows) are forced so that each of those rows has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s, and similarly the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th row (for the first [latex]3[/latex] columns) are forced by the column parity condition. The single remaining corner entry (row [latex]4[/latex], column [latex]4[/latex]) is then also forced, and it is easy to check the row-[latex]4[/latex] parity and column-[latex]4[/latex] parity conditions become consistent automatically.

So the count of valid matrices [latex]=2^{(4-1)^2}=2^9=512[/latex].

Answer: 512

questions.text:
Consider a system of linear equations [latex]P X = Q [/latex] where [latex]P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} [/latex] and [latex]Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1} [/latex]. Suppose [latex]P [/latex] has an [latex]LU [/latex] decomposition, [latex]P = LU [/latex], where

[latex] L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Solving via [latex]LY=Q[/latex] then [latex]UX=Y[/latex]: substituting [latex]P=LU[/latex] into [latex]PX=Q[/latex] gives [latex]L(UX)=Q[/latex]; setting [latex]Y=UX[/latex], we solve [latex]LY=Q[/latex] first (easy, forward substitution since [latex]L[/latex] is lower triangular), then [latex]UX=Y[/latex] (easy, back substitution). True — this is exactly the standard LU-solve method.

If [latex]P[/latex] is invertible, both [latex]L,U[/latex] invertible: [latex]L[/latex] is unit lower-triangular (diagonal all [latex]1[/latex]s), so [latex]\det(L)=1[/latex] always, regardless of [latex]P[/latex] — [latex]L[/latex] is always invertible. Since [latex]\det(P)=\det(L)\det(U)=\det(U)[/latex], if [latex]P[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det(P)\ne0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)\ne0[/latex] too. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] singular, some diagonal element of [latex]U[/latex] is zero: since [latex]\det(P)=\det(U)[/latex] (product of [latex]U[/latex]'s diagonal, as [latex]U[/latex] is upper triangular), if [latex]P[/latex] is singular ([latex]\det(P)=0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)=0[/latex], which for a triangular matrix forces at least one diagonal entry to be [latex]0[/latex]. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] symmetric, both [latex]L,U[/latex] symmetric: plain LU decomposition does not generally preserve/reveal symmetry in [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]U[/latex] individually (that requires a specialized decomposition like [latex]LDL^T[/latex] or Cholesky). False in general.

Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (about symmetric P forcing symmetric L,U) is FALSE.

Click here for detail solution
options: The system [latex]P X = Q [/latex] can be solved by first solving [latex]L Y = Q [/latex] and then [latex]U X = Y [/latex].
If [latex]P [/latex] is invertible, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are invertible.
If [latex]P [/latex] is singular, then at least one of the diagonal elements of [latex]U [/latex] is zero.
If [latex]P [/latex] is symmetric, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are symmetric.
